title: Scaling PostgreSQL to power 800 million ChatGPT users
quotes: The system (initially created by a team of scientists at University of California, Berkeley) has enabled us to support massive global traffic with a single primary Azure PostgreSQL flexible server instance
Over the past year, our PostgreSQL load has grown by more than 10x, and it continues to rise quickly.
We also no longer allow adding new tables to the current PostgreSQL deployment. New workloads default to the sharded systems.
This also cuts connection setup latency: in our benchmarks, the average connection time dropped from 50 milliseconds (ms) to 5 ms.
We operate nearly 50 read replicas across multiple geographic regions to minimize latency.
We enforce a strict 5-second timeout on schema changes.
We consistently deliver low double-digit millisecond p99 client-side latency and five-nines availability in production.
For example, we once identified an extremely costly query that joined 12 tables, where spikes in this query were responsible for past high-severity SEVs.

numbers.t: PostgreSQL load growth over the past year
single primary instance serving all writes
max connections per Azure PostgreSQL instance (see note)
replicas possible with cascading replication, in testing (see note)
tables joined by one SEV-causing query
SEV-0 PostgreSQL incident in 12 months (ImageGen launch, writes up >10x, 100M+ signups in a week; see note)

summary: OpenAI runs ChatGPT and the API on one unsharded Azure PostgreSQL primary with nearly 50 read replicas in several regions, at millions of QPS. They climbed the ladder as far as scale-up plus read replicas, PgBouncer pooling, a caching layer with cache locking, workload isolation onto separate instances, and multi-layer rate limiting. Shardable write-heavy workloads moved to sharded systems (Azure Cosmos DB), new tables are forbidden in Postgres, and only lightweight schema changes with a 5-second timeout are allowed. Cascading replication is being tested to go past about 100 replicas.
note: Fetched via r.jina.ai reader (openai.com returns 403 to direct fetch); date and author (Bohan Zhang, Member of the Technical Staff) from a Wayback copy. The only SEV-0 in 12 months was during the ChatGPT ImageGen launch: 'write traffic suddenly surged by more than 10x as over 100 million new users signed up within a week' (verbatim from the post). The '800 million' figure is from the title. Further verbatim lines: 'Each instance has a maximum connection limit (5,000 in Azure PostgreSQL).' and 'This approach allows us to scale to potentially over a hundred replicas without overwhelming the primary.'. Other text in the post: caching layer with cache locking and leasing; PgBouncer in statement or transaction mode; HA hot standby; rate limiting at application, connection pooler, proxy and query layers; ORM can block specific query digests; backfills rate-limited and can take over a week.

New tables are no longer allowed in Postgres. For feature additions that require new tables, use alternative systems.
Sharding current workloads in Postgres is difficult due to the complexity of migrating hundreds of application endpoints.
Added dozens of read replicas with no increase in replication lag
Only one SEV-0 incident involving PostgreSQL in the past 9 months
Increased Read Replica Lags (> 10 mins)

summary: Conference talk preceding the January 2026 blog post. Same architecture: one Azure Postgres primary, many replicas, write-heavy shardable workloads moved elsewhere, no new tables. Its outage case studies show the failure modes of the replica step: a write spike pushed primary CPU to 90%+ and replica lag past 10 minutes, and a WAL sender bug plus network saturation on the primary kept lag growing after writes were rate limited.

title: Herding elephants: lessons learned from sharding Postgres at Notion
quotes: By mid-2020, it was clear that product usage would surpass the abilities of our trusty Postgres monolith, which had served us dutifully through five years and four orders of magnitude of growth.
For us, the inflection point arrived when the Postgres `VACUUM` process began to stall consistently, preventing the database from reclaiming disk space from dead tuples.
We needed at least 60K total IOPS to meet existing demand, with the capacity to scale further if needed.
To keep Postgres humming and preserve RDS replication guarantees, we set an upper bound of 500 GB per table and 10 TB per physical database.
After crunching the numbers, we settled on an architecture consisting of **480 logical shards** evenly distributed across **32 physical databases**.
For example, in the future we could scale from 32 to 40 to 48 hosts, making incremental jumps each time.
With all 96 CPUs (!) on the `m5.24xlarge` instance we provisioned, our final script took around three days to backfill the production environment.

numbers.t: max per table / per physical DB

summary: Notion sharded its single RDS Postgres monolith in 2021 because VACUUM stalled and TXID wraparound loomed. They chose application-level sharding by workspace ID into 480 logical shards (Postgres schemas, 15 per database) on 32 physical databases, rejecting Citus and Vitess for control. Migration: audit-log double writes, backfill, verification with dark reads, then a five-minute maintenance window. This is the 'shard by tenant' step of the ladder.
note: The post picks 480 because it has many factors (vs 512, which would force doubling hosts). The 15-per-database and 5-minute figures are in the post ('15 per database, 480 total'; 'took Notion down for five minutes of scheduled maintenance').

title: The Great Re-shard: adding Postgres capacity (again) with zero downtime
quotes: Some of the shards were exceeding 90% CPU utilization at peak traffic
After going through a capacity planning exercise, we landed on tripling the number of instances in our fleet from 32 to 96 machines.
Since we chose a scaling factor of 3x, we went from having 15 schemas per shard to 5.
Total time to synchronize the machines decreased from **3 days to 12 hours!**

Specifically, we had about 100 PgBouncer instances, each of which could open up to 6 connections to each space shard (as well as some connections to other unsharded databases), for a total of 600 connections to each shard.
The solution was to first shard our PgBouncer cluster.

At worst, a user would have experienced about a second of a “saving” loading spinner while the failover was waiting for queries to finish, updating configs, swapping the replication stream, and reloading our proxy layer to send queries to the new shards.

numbers.t: peak CPU on some shards before
sync time after skipping index builds during copy
PgBouncer shard groups x databases each (see note)
CPU and IOPS at peak after

summary: In 2023 Notion tripled its space-shard fleet from 32 to 96 Postgres machines without downtime, keeping the 480 logical shards and moving 5 schemas per new machine. Data was copied with Postgres logical replication (indexes built after copy), verified with dark reads, and cut over per database by pausing PgBouncer, with reverse replication for rollback. PgBouncer itself had to be sharded into 4 groups first. This is the 'reshard by moving logical shards' step.
note: PgBouncer split: the post says it split the space shards into '4 groups, with 24 databases downstream of each PgBouncer shard' (fragment, verbatim; the full sentence contains a dash). After-state figure from an image caption in the post: 'New CPU and IOPS utilization hovers around 20% during peak traffic' (verbatim, not in quotes list).

title: How Notion build and grew our data lake to keep up with rapid growth
quotes: At the start of 2021 we had more than 20 billion block rows in Postgres, and this figure has since grown to more than two hundred billion blocks
Thus we maintained a total of 480 logical shards while ensuring long-term scalable data management and retrieval capabilities.
We set up one Debezium CDC connector per Postgres host and deploy them in an AWS EKS cluster.
summary: Confirms the shard history (32 instances x 15 logical shards in 2021, 96 x 5 in 2023, 480 logical shards throughout) and the data growth behind it. Shows the analytics side effect of sharding: one CDC connector per Postgres host feeding Kafka and a Hudi data lake, after 480 per-shard Fivetran connectors became unmanageable.
note: Title is verbatim as published ('build', sic). Quote 1 is a verbatim fragment; the sentence continues 'a data volume of hundreds of terabytes, even when compressed.' 96 x 5 figure: 'continued in 2023 by increasing the number of physical instances to 96, with five logical shards per instance' (in the post).

title: The growing pains of database architecture
quotes: In 2020, Figma’s infrastructure hit some growing pains due to a combination of new features, preparing to launch a second product, and more users (database traffic grows approximately 3x annually).
Most visibly, we observed upwards of 65% CPU utilization during peak traffic due to the volume of queries serviced by one database.
Additionally, not all reads or data fetching could be moved to replicas due to application sensitivity to replication lag.
Instead of splitting each table across many databases, we would move _groups of tables_ onto their own databases.
By removing indexes in the destination database and rebuilding the indexes after the initial copying of data, we reduced the copy time to a matter of hours.
Our first operation involved moving two high-traffic tables, while our final operation in October 2022 involved 50.
During each operation, we observed a ~30 second period of partial availability impact (~2% of requests dropped).
Our largest partition has CPU utilization hovering ~10%, and we’ve decreased the resources allocated to some of the lower traffic partitions.

numbers.t: peak CPU on the single RDS database
tables moved in first vs final partition operation

summary: Figma's first moves on one RDS Postgres: scale up to the largest instance (r5.12xlarge to r5.24xlarge), add read replicas, put new use cases on new databases, add PgBouncer. Writes and lag-sensitive reads still loaded the primary, so they vertically partitioned groups of tables onto separate databases using logical replication and a PgBouncer pause-and-reroute, with under a minute of impact per move. This is the 'vertical partitioning' step before sharding.
note: The upgrade list is verbatim in the post: 'Upgrade our database to the largest instance available (from r5.12xlarge to r5.24xlarge) to maximize CPU utilization runway'.

title: How Figma’s databases team lived to tell the scale
quotes: Figma’s database stack has grown almost 100x since 2020.

In 2020, we were running a single Postgres database hosted on AWS’s largest physical instance, and by the end of 2022, we had built out a distributed architecture with caching, read replicas, and a dozen vertically partitioned databases.
The data revealed that some of our tables, containing several terabytes and billions of rows, were becoming too large for a single database.
Our highest write tables were growing so quickly that we would soon exceed the maximum IO operations per second (IOPS) supported by Amazon’s Relational Database Service (RDS).
During our evaluation, we explored CockroachDB, TiDB, Spanner, and Vitess.
We shipped our first horizontally sharded table in September 2023.
We successfully failed over with only ten seconds of partial availability on database primaries and no availability impact on replicas.

numbers.t: vertically partitioned databases by end of 2022
tables too large for one database
partial availability on primaries at failover
of queries supported by the DBProxy subset

summary: When single tables outgrew one RDS instance (vacuum trouble, IOPS ceiling), Figma built horizontal sharding on top of RDS Postgres instead of migrating to CockroachDB, TiDB, Spanner or Vitess. Key ideas: colos (groups of tables sharing a shard key), logical sharding via Postgres views before physical splits, and DBProxy, a Go query router with scatter-gather and load shedding. This is the 'shard it yourself behind a proxy' step.
note: '<10%' from: 'views would only add a minimal performance overhead in most cases, and less than 10% in the worst cases'. '90%' from: 'we picked a query language that supported the most common 90% of queries'. Both verbatim in the post.

title: Sharding & IDs at Instagram
quotes: Our sharded system consists of several thousand ‘logical’ shards that are mapped in code to far fewer physical shards.
Each ‘logical’ shard is a Postgres schema in our system, and each sharded table (for example, likes on our photos) exists inside each schema.
41 bits for time in milliseconds (gives us 41 years of IDs with a custom epoch)
13 bits that represent the logical shard ID
10 bits that represent an auto-incrementing sequence, modulus 1024. This means we can generate 1024 IDs, per shard, per millisecond
summary: Instagram sharded Postgres by mapping several thousand logical shards (Postgres schemas) onto a few physical servers, so moving a logical shard rebalances without rehashing. IDs are 64-bit and generated inside Postgres with PL/pgSQL: time, logical shard ID and a per-table sequence. The classic logical-shard pattern Notion later copied.
note: Fetched from a Wayback Machine copy of the Medium page (2023 snapshot). The Medium page shows 'Dec 30, 2012'; the post first ran on Instagram's earlier engineering blog in 2012 (original date not confirmed here). Later Instagram Postgres scaling talks not searched (search budget exhausted).

title: How Discord Stores Billions of Messages
quotes: Around November 2015, we reached 100 million stored messages and at this time we started to see the expected issues appearing: the data and the index could no longer fit in RAM and latencies started to become unpredictable.
We decided to bucket our messages by time.
We looked at the largest channels on Discord and determined if we stored about 10 days of messages within a bucket that we could comfortably stay under 100MB.
Cassandra partition keys can be compounded, so our new primary key became ((channel_id, bucket), message_id).
We are currently running a 12 node cluster with a replica factor of 3 and will just continue to add new Cassandra nodes as needed.
We currently store nearly 1TB of compressed data on each node.

numbers.t: stored messages when MongoDB stopped fitting in RAM (Nov 2015)

summary: Discord moved messages from a single MongoDB replica set to Cassandra once data and index outgrew RAM. The partition key is (channel_id, bucket) where a bucket is a 10-day window, bounding partitions under about 100 MB. Not SQL, but the clearest example of choosing a partition key that keeps each query on one partition and bounds partition size.
note: Discord's page metadata now shows a 2026 republish date; the byline date on the page is January 13, 2017 (author Stanislav Vishnevskiy). '120 million' from: 'as of this blog post we are well past 120 million' (messages a day).

title: How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages
quotes: In 2017, we ran 12 Cassandra nodes, storing billions of messages.
At the beginning of 2022, it had 177 nodes with trillions of messages.
If multiple users are requesting the same row at the same time, we’ll only query the database once.
We turn it on and leave it running, migrating messages at speeds of up to 3.2 million per second.
Each ScyllaDB node has 9 TB of disk space, up from the average of 4 TB per Cassandra node.

For example, fetching historical messages had a p99 of between 40-125ms on Cassandra, with ScyllaDB having a nice and chill 15ms p99 latency, and message insert performance going from 5-70ms p99 on Cassandra, to a steady 5ms p99 on ScyllaDB.
summary: By 2022 the messages Cassandra cluster had grown to 177 nodes with trillions of messages and hot partitions. Discord added Rust data services with request coalescing and consistent-hash routing by channel, then migrated to 72 ScyllaDB nodes in May 2022. Shows that the partition key remains the scaling unit and that hot partitions need coalescing above the database.
note: Page metadata shows a 2026 date; the byline on the page reads 'March 6, 2023'. 177 -> 72 from: 'we’re going from running 177 Cassandra nodes to just 72 ScyllaDB nodes' (verbatim fragment; the full sentence contains a dash so it is not in quotes). Cutover: 'We switched our messages database over in May 2022'.

title: Partitioning GitHub’s relational databases to handle scale
quotes: To do that, we group database tables that belong together into schema domains and enforce boundaries between the domains with SQL linters.
The query linter verifies that only tables belonging to the same schema domain can be referenced in the same database query.
We moved 130 of our busiest tables at once––those that power GitHub’s core features: repositories, issues, and pull requests.
In 2019, `mysql1` answered 950,000 queries/s on average, 900,000 queries/s on replicas, and 50,000 queries/s on the primary.
All hosts of these clusters combined answer 1,200,000 queries/s on average (1,125,000 queries/s on replicas, 75,000 queries/s on the primaries).
At the same time, the average load on each host halved.

numbers.t: busiest tables moved in one write cutover
load reduction on hosts with former mysql1 data

summary: GitHub split its main MySQL cluster (mysql1) by feature: tables grouped into schema domains, with query and transaction linters enforcing that nothing spans domains (virtual partitions), then moved physically with Vitess vertical sharding or a custom read-only write-cutover. The read share is striking: about 95% of mysql1 queries went to replicas. This is the 'functional (vertical) partitioning' step.
note: Quote 3 keeps the source's two en-dashes (U+2013 x2) after 'at once'; no em-dash. '50%' from: 'The result, we see in 2021, is a 50% load reduction on database hosts housing the data that once was on mysql1.' The '1,200 MySQL hosts' figure is from the 2023 post, not this one.

title: Upgrading GitHub.com to MySQL 8.0
quotes: Our fleet consists of 1200+ hosts. It’s a combination of Azure Virtual Machines and bare metal hosts in our data center.
We store 300+ TB of data and serve 5.5 million queries per second across 50+ database clusters.
Each cluster is configured for high availability with a primary plus replicas cluster setup.
We also have horizontally sharded Vitess clusters for large-domain areas that outgrew the single-primary MySQL cluster.
The last time GitHub upgraded MySQL versions, we had five database clusters and now we have 50+ clusters.
summary: By late 2023 GitHub ran 1200+ MySQL hosts in 50+ primary-plus-replica clusters serving 5.5 million QPS, mostly split by product domain, with Vitess horizontal sharding only for domains that outgrew one primary. Shows the end state of the ladder for most companies: many functional clusters, sharding only where needed.
note: Page shows 'December 7, 2023 | Updated May 21, 2024'. Markdown link syntax removed from quotes 3 and 4 (link text kept).

title: A Pods Architecture To Allow Shopify To Scale
quotes: In 2015, it was no longer possible to continue buying a larger database server for Shopify.
We finally had no choice but to shard the database, which allowed us to horizontally scale our databases and continue our growth.
A pod consists of a set of shops that live on a fully isolated set of datastores.
We developed a tool called the Pod Mover to allow us to move a pod to its recovery data center in a minute without dropping requests or jobs.

numbers.t: year scale-up ran out and sharding began
pod failover to recovery data center

summary: Shopify sharded MySQL by shop in 2015 when it could no longer buy a bigger server, then in 2016 turned each shard into a fully isolated pod (MySQL plus Redis and Memcached) so one shard's failure could not take down the platform. A load-balancer component (Sorting Hat) routes each request to its pod. This is 'shard by tenant, then isolate cells'.
note: Date from the page's datePublished meta (2018-03-02).

title: Shard Balancing: Moving Shops Confidently with Zero-Downtime at Terabyte-scale
quotes: A pod is an isolated instance of Shopify consisting of an individual MySQL database shard, along with other datastores like Redis and Memcached.
The least used shard and most used shard vary by almost four times and the deviation across all shards is too large.
To perform the data migration, we use a library called Ghostferry: an open-source tool, built in-house, designed to copy data from one MySQL instance to another.
Ghostferry uses two main components to copy over data: batch copying and tailing the binlog.
The routing table is updated to associate the shop with its _new_ pod.
The only opportunity for downtime is during the cutover.

numbers.t: spread between least and most used shard before balancing

summary: Shops land on arbitrary shards and grow unevenly, so Shopify rebalances by moving individual shops between MySQL shards online. Ghostferry batch-copies the shop's rows and tails the binlog, then a short cutover under a Redis-backed lock updates the routing table. This is the 'rebalance hot tenants' step after sharding.
note: '~2x' from: 'The range between the least used shard and most used shard is now closer to two times.' No terabyte count or move count given beyond the title. Date from datePublished meta.

title: Scaling Datastores at Slack with Vitess
quotes: Our migration to Vitess began in 2017 and Vitess now serves 99% of our overall query load.
Today, we serve 2.3 million QPS at peak. 2M of those queries are reads and 300K are writes. Our median query latency is 2 ms, and our p99 query latency is 11 ms.
All the data for a given workspace was stored on the same shard, so the application just needed to connect to that one database.
However, there was a fundamental limitation with the scaling model. **What if a single team and all of their Slack data doesn’t fit our largest shard?**
In the fall of 2016, we were dealing with hundreds of thousands of MySQL queries per second and thousands of sharded MySQL hosts in production.
For example, instead of putting all the messages from every channel and DM on a given workspace into the same shard, we wanted to shard the message data by the unique id of the channel.
On the datastores side, in just one week we saw query rates increase by 50%.
summary: Slack originally sharded MySQL by workspace on active-active pairs, which hit hot spots and could not hold its largest customers or cross-workspace features. From 2017 it moved to Vitess, resharding data by other keys (for example messages by channel ID), and by late 2020 Vitess served 99% of queries at 2.3M peak QPS. This is the 'outgrew tenant sharding, adopt a sharding middleware' step.
note: Date from the page byline (December 1, 2020). 'six total regions' from: 'we run Vitess clusters in six total regions'. Host count after Vitess not given.

title: Evolving Schemaless into a Distributed SQL Database; How Uber Serves Over 40 Million Reads Per Second from Online Storage Using an Integrated Cache
quotes: Docstore is a general-purpose multi-model database that provides a strict serializability consistency model on a partition level and can scale horizontally to serve high volume workloads.

Typically, there are multiple partitions in each Docstore instance. To eliminate a single point of failure, a partition is a group of 3-5 nodes and each node is a unit of physical isolation and is deployed to an independent zone.
To ensure consistency, each partition runs the raft consensus protocol.
Docstore uses MySQL as the underlying database engine.
Storing tens of PBs of data and serving tens of millions of requests/second, it is one of the largest database engines at Uber used by microservices from all business verticals.
Today CacheFront supports over 40M requests per second across all Docstore instances in production, and the number is growing.
In fact, one of our largest initial use cases drives over 6M RPS with a 99% cache hit rate with a proven successful failover where all traffic was redirected to the remote region.

numbers.t: one use case, cache hit rate
storage-engine CPU vs Redis cores for that use case

summary: Uber's Docstore is in-house distributed SQL: tables are sharded into partitions of 3-5 MySQL nodes across zones, each partition replicated with Raft, giving strict serializability within a partition. It stores tens of petabytes and serves tens of millions of requests per second, with an integrated Redis cache (CacheFront) absorbing 40M+ reads per second. This is the 'distributed SQL' end of the ladder, built rather than bought.
note: Two Uber posts: schemaless-sql-database (2021-02-23, quotes 1 to 4) and https://www.uber.com/blog/how-uber-serves-over-40-million-reads-per-second-using-an-integrated-cache/ (2024-02-15, quotes 5 to 7). Dates read from the pages' HTML via r.jina.ai (direct fetch blocked). '60K -> 3K' from: 'would have originally required approximately 60K CPU cores in order to serve 6M RPS from the storage engine directly' and 'only 3K Redis cores'. title: Read replica limits and replication lag on RDS for PostgreSQL and Aurora
quotes: The maximum number of read replicas per primary DB instance.

For cascading read replicas, RDS for PostgreSQL supports 15 read replicas for each source DB instance at first level of replication, and 5 read replicas for each source DB instance at the second and third level of replication.
You can create a series of up to three read replicas in a chain from a source RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance.
An Aurora DB cluster can contain up to 15 Aurora Replicas.
This lag is usually much less than 100 milliseconds after the primary instance has written an update.
Amazon RDS then uses the asynchronous replication method for the DB engine to update the read replica whenever there is a change to the primary DB instance.
If no user transactions are running on the source DB instance, the associated PostgreSQL read replica reports a replication lag of up to five minutes.

numbers.t: read replicas per primary (RDS quota table: 'Read replicas per primary | Each supported Region: 15')
cascading replicas per source at levels 1, 2, 3
max cascade depth (chain of at most 4 instances)
reported RDS PG lag when idle (WAL switch)

summary: RDS for PostgreSQL allows 15 read replicas per primary, and cascading replicas (PostgreSQL 14.1+) up to three levels deep with 5 per source at levels two and three. Aurora allows 15 Aurora Replicas per cluster sharing one storage volume, with lag usually under 100 ms. RDS replication is asynchronous, so replica lag is a property of the design, not a fault.
note: Quote 1 is the description column of the quota row 'Read replicas per primary | Each supported Region: 15 | Yes (adjustable)' in CHAP_Limits.html; the same row says 'This quota cant be adjusted for Amazon Aurora.' 'published' is the access date; AWS docs are living pages.
